passages.text: Illuminating the monoamine transporters: fluorescently labeled ligands to study DAT, SERT, and NET

Fluorescence microscopy has revolutionized the visualization of physiological processes in live-cell systems. With the recent innovations in super resolution microscopy, these events can be examined with high precision and accuracy. The development of fluorescently labeled small molecules has provided a significant advance in understanding the physiological relevance of targeted proteins that can now be visualized at the cellular level. One set of physiologically important target proteins are the monoamine transporters (MATs) that play an instrumental role in maintaining monoamine signaling homeostasis. Understanding the mechanisms underlying their regulation and dysregulation is fundamental to treating several neuropsychiatric conditions such as attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), anxiety, depression and substance use disorders. Herein, we describe the rationale behind the small molecule design of fluorescently labeled ligands (FLL) either as MAT substrates or inhibitors as well as their applications to advance our understanding of this class of transporters in health and disease.
INTRODUCTION

The dopamine transporter (DAT) as well as the serotonin and the norepinephrine transporters (SERT and NET, respectively) are the three homologous members of the monoamine transporter (MAT) uptake-1 system and belong to a branch of the one of the largest solute carrier families (SLC), the SLC6. Their main function is to terminate biogenic monoamine signaling by mediating the re-uptake of released dopamine (DA), serotonin (5-HT) or norepinephrine (NE) from the extracellular space into the cell by a similar mechanism, which is Na+ and Cl- dependent. Dysregulation of these transporters has been linked to mood, cognitive, sleep and substance use disorders. For example, DAT was identified 35 years ago as the main target of cocaine's psychostimulant action and addictive liability. Although, there is still no FDA approved pharmacotherapy for cocaine use disorder, there are a wide variety of FDA approved drugs targeting these proteins to treat ADHD, depression, anxiety and sleep disorders. Playing a supportive role in the clearance of biogenic amines, the uptake-2 transporter system includes the organic cation transporters (OCTs) and the plasma membrane monoamine transporters (PMAT). Compared to the MAT uptake-1 system, the uptake-2 transporters have a lower affinity and a high capacity for monoamine transport. These transporters belong to the SLC2 family, and they are not Na+ and Cl- dependent. Unlike the uptake-1 transporters, the availability of selective ligands to study these transporters is limited even though they have arisen as potential targets for neuropsychiatric disorders such as depression, and substance use disorders. Recent structural insights might shed light on the future generation of selective MAT uptake-2 compounds.

Fluorescent microscopy has emerged as a pioneering technique to visualize and study distinct living systems, opening research opportunities and increasing our knowledge of real-time physiological processes, which will enable a better understanding of the function and dysfunction of a specific protein of interest that will ultimately lead to better therapeutics. The use of genetically encoded biosensors to monitor dynamic interactions in living cells and in in vivo models, has revolutionized the visualization of neurotransmitter dynamics but are not always suitable for animal models in which genetic manipulation is impossible, e.g., nonhuman primates. Alternatively, the development of small molecule fluorescently labeled ligands (FLL) is an approach that utilizes a "parent ligand" which will bind non-covalently to the protein of interest, usually in the orthosteric binding site and will serve as the "carrier" of a covalently tethered fluorophore. This technique avoids genetic manipulation and has been used in cultured cell systems and brain slices across different species. The use of FLL is not limited to the study of protein expression and distribution in cells and tissue. It can extend to the investigation of oligomerization, internalization and downstream signaling processes, binding properties and as a fluorescent couple in FRET or BRET assays.

Structurally, one approach that has been utilized for the design of FLL for DAT, SERT and NET and other proteins of interest includes the use of three components: 1) a high affinity and MAT selective parent ligand, 2) an optimal length linker of appropriate physicochemical composition and 3) an appropriate fluorescent dye (Figure 1). Structure-activity relationship (SAR) information on the parent ligand is critically important as this will identify the best position for addition of the sterically bulky fluorophore as well as tolerability of linker length. In most cases, addition of the fluorescent tag adversely affects binding affinity and thus minimizing this decrease by choosing a position on the parent ligand that will have the least impact is critical to success. In addition, SAR findings will provide guidance for the design of the synthetic scheme to obtain the final FLL, that usually requires the addition of the fluorescent label as the final step. This approach has generated a variety of fluorescent inhibitors of uptake-1 MATs. Recent reports suggest that the linker length and composition contributes to the binding affinity and selectivity of the FLL. Computational analyses have revealed that the linker and fluorescent dye in some cases, preferentially extend outside of the orthosteric binding site, interacting with amino acid residues and affecting protein conformation that may play a role in the binding affinity and selectivity of the FLL. Importantly, the linker length and composition (i.e. PEG or alkyl chain) will affect both the biophysical and binding properties of the FLL. Finally, selection of the fluorescent dye must take into consideration target location and fluorophore properties, for instance, whether the target protein resides at the surface of the plasma membrane or if the FLL has to permeate into the cytoplasm to have access to the targeted protein. For more details with regard to fluorophore characteristics, Grimm and Lavis recently published a detailed review highlighting pros and cons of distinct fluorescent dyes.

A second approach that has been explored, is the generation of fluorescent ligands that mimic an endogenous or exogenous substrate. These molecules tend to be less bulky and therefore, transport is facilitated. In this mini review we will summarize the structural design rational of fluorescent ligands substrates and inhibitors as well as their use and application to increase our knowledge of uptake-1 biogenic amine transport. Although the scope of this mini review is to focus on uptake-1 MAT FLL, we acknowledge that there is an overlap with some of the fluorescent substrates used to study uptake-2 MATs.
MONOAMINE TRANSPORTERS
Dopamine transporter (DAT)

Prior to the utilization of FLL, radiolabeled substrates and inhibitors were used to study DAT regulation. 4-(4-Dimethylaminostyryl)-N-methylpyridinium (ASP+) was the first fluorescent substrate reported, that applied fluorescent technology to study MAT distribution, activity and regulation (Figure 2a). Although, initially utilized to study NET, it was subsequently shown to also be a substrate of DAT and SERT. This compound is an analogue of the neurotoxin 1-methyl-4-phenylpyridinium (MPP+), a substrate for DAT, NET and SERT and a metabolite of 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP) that has been used in Parkinson's disease models due to its neurotoxic profile. One advantage to using ASP+ as a fluorescent substrate instead of [3H]DA for uptake experiments is highlighted in two studies by Bolan et al. and Zapata et al. where ASP+ was utilized to assess the role of D2R and D3R receptors in the regulation of DAT function and surface expression in heterologous expression systems. In both studies co-expression of D2R or D3R with DAT was required. The utilization of [3H]DA would have been problematic, as this substrate is not only transported by DAT but also can bind and activate these dopaminergic receptors. In contrast, it was demonstrated that ASP+ did not activate D2R or D3R.

An interesting approach to visualize uptake and release on presynaptic terminals has been achieved by the development of fluorescent false neurotransmitters (FFNs). As indicated by their name, the structural design of these ligands is based on simulating the endogenous neurotransmitters. This was achieved by: 1) replacing the aromatic moiety present in biogenic amines for a fluorescent coumarin core and, 2) attaching an amino ethyl group to the fluorescent moiety to ensure similar interactions with the transporters. In addition, photophysical and physicochemical properties played a key role in the development of these pH-dependent fluorescent molecules. Initially, FFNs were utilized to trace neurotransmitter release, as many of the first developed probes were substrates of both, vesicular monoamine transporter 1 and 2 (VMAT1, VMAT2, respectively). Rodriguez et al. demonstrated that FFN102 (Figure 2b) was a mouse DAT substrate, in addition to its interaction with VMAT-2. One limitation of FFN102 is that although it is an effective probe to be used in mouse brain slices and it has been utilized to study neurotransmission in distinct regions of the mouse brain, it failed to be useful in cultured neurons, as accumulation of this probe was not observed. Additionally, the authors report a low affinity for human DAT.

Due to low expression and the lack of appropriate tools to study endogenous DAT expression in living neurons, most of the DAT trafficking and distribution studies were previously done in non-neuronal transfected cells. Two fluorescent cocaine-based analogues, JHC1-064 and MFZ9-18, (Figure 1 and Figure 2c) were the first reported FLL to overcome these limitations providing the necessary tools to visualize trafficking of DAT in primary cultures of rat dopaminergic neurons (Figure 3). The structural differences between these two FLL resides in the fluorescent tag (Figure 1 and Figure 2c), while JHC1-064 was labeled with rhodamine red-X, MFZ9-18 was tagged at the same position with Oregon Green. This exchange of fluorophores had a small effect on [3H]dopamine uptake inhibition in COS-7 cells transiently transfected with hDAT, with JHC1-064 showing a slightly a higher affinity than MFZ9-18 (Ki = 62 nM and 142 nM, respectively). Initially, JHC1-064 was inspired by RTI-233 (Figure 2d), a cocaine-based analogue that was originally developed to study SERT. Structurally, RTI-233 was tagged at the 2beta position of the parent ligand RTI-374 (Figure 2e) and the fluorescent label nitrobenzoxadiazole (NBD) was appended. For JHC1-064 and MF9-18, MFZ2-12 (Figure 2f) was chosen as parent ligand since it had previously been reported to bind with high affinity to DAT and [3H]MFZ2-12 proved to be an exceptionally high affinity radioligand. While substitution in the 2- position of MFZ-2-12 with rhodamine red-X fluorescent dye was well tolerated, substitution in the N- position yielded JHC1-064 with higher affinity for DAT. In addition, this compound demonstrated greater photostability and quantum yield when compared to RTI-233.

An interesting characteristic of JHC1-064 is that although it is a non-covalent and theoretically reversible FLL, it possesses a slow rate of dissociation. This unexpected property served to visualize the internalization of JHC1-064-labeled DAT and compare two systems: DAT-HEK293 transfected cells and endogenously expressed DAT in neurons. Internalization of DAT in heterologous systems was known to be mediated by activation of protein kinase C (PKC) and this was confirmed and visualized with JHC1-064 in HEK293-DAT transfected cells. Nevertheless, when compared to endogenous DAT expressed in dopaminergic neurons, JHC1-064 revealed a constitutively-induced internalization mechanism, where activation of PKC did not play a fundamental role, at least under these conditions. The following year Eriksen et al. utilized JHC1-064 to investigate the final destination of constitutively internalized DAT and whether this fate was the same in heterologous expression systems such as HEK293-DAT cells compared to DAT expressed in dopaminergic neurons. Since these initial studies, JHC1-064 has been utilized as a powerful tool to investigate DAT trafficking regulation and surface expression. In brief, JHC1-064 was utilized to study DAT internalization by KCl-induced membrane depolarization, DAT expression and targeted conformation in filopodia, DAT constitutive internalization in neurons in the presence of methyl-beta-cyclodextrin, revealing that DAT clustering is cholesterol-dependent, expression and distribution of DAT mutants associated with ADHD and Parkinson's disease. Nevertheless, a limitation of JHC1-064 has been its high lipophilicity, which has been a contributing factor for non-specific labeling when utilized in brain slices of distinct species. As this property is influenced by the fluorophore, the Oregon Green analogue, MFZ9-18, which is more hydrophilic was successfully utilized to label dopaminergic axons in rhesus macaque brain tissue slices.

So far, JHC1-064 (Figure 1) has been the most widely used FLL to study DAT and has served as a model for the design of new generation FLL. These DAT FLL are better suited for super resolution microscopy experiments, such as direct stochastic optical reconstruction microscopy (dSTORM). For these FLL, JHC1-064 was modified by replacing the fluorescent dye and the length and composition of the linker. The rhodamine-red dye was replaced by the Janelia Fluor dyes JF549 and JF646 and to counterbalance the high lipophilicity of the JF dyes, PEG of different lengths or a piperazine linker were explored. As a result, four novel fluorescent ligands were developed where DG3-80 (Figure 2g) had the highest affinity for rDAT (Ki = 6 nM) followed by DG4-91 (Figure 2h, rDAT Ki = 28 nM). There was no apparent relationship between DAT affinity and the PEG linker length. When compared to JHC1-064, these compounds have similar affinities for DAT and SERT, although there is a decrease in affinity for NET. These four fluorescent ligands were tested to determine their capacity to specifically label DAT by confocal microscopy and by total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) on the surface of CAD cells transiently transfected with enhanced green fluorescent protein-tagged hDAT (EGFP-hDAT) and in dopaminergic neurons. Of the four tested compounds, DG3-80 and DG4-91 demonstrated specific surface labeling of DAT in both systems. DG3-80 has recently been used for dSTORM experiments revealing a mechanism for rapid alterations in nanoscopic DAT distribution, demonstrating a remarkable link to the conformational state of the transporter in both cultured neurons and mouse striatal slices.
Serotonin transporter (SERT)

Initial FLL development targeting SERT was first described with the high affinity cocaine analogue RTI-374 (Figure 2d), yielding RTI-233 (Figure 2c) which was the first reported high affinity FLL binding to rSERT, as revealed by its binding affinity (Ki= 6 nM) in rSERT expressed in SF-9 insect cell membranes and in purified rSERT (Ki= 14 nM). An interesting characteristic of this FLL is the presence of NBD as the fluorescent dye, since the fluorescent properties of this fluorescent label are influenced by the solvent environment allowing the utilization of this FLL as a reporter to study the binding pocket environmental characteristics of rSERT.

As described above, another approach for the development of FLL is the utilization of a fluorescent molecule that is structurally related to the endogenous neurotransmitter. This approach was explored by Micotto et al. where they reported a series of fluorescent 5-HT analogues based on 6-hydroxycarbostyril. The four final fluorescent compounds were screened to assess their ability to mimic the actions of 5-HT in cultured neurons and astroglia. Reuptake of two of the final compounds was diminished in the presence of the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) clomipramine (compound 1 and 4 in Micotto et al. Figure 4a-b) suggesting their actions as SERT substrates.

In a similar approach, the same group reported the synthesis of ethylamine-functionalized fluorescent probes by using naphthalene, anthracene, pyrene and phenothiazine as the fluorophore cores. Based on physical and photophysical properties of all final compounds, compound 5 (Figure 4c) was suitable for cellular and in vivo studies and showed accumulation in a MLO-Y4 (Murine osteocyte) cell line expressing SERT. In the presence of clomipramine, uptake of this FLL was significantly reduced.

We previously described ASP+ (4-(4-(dimethylamino)-styryl)-N-methylpyridinium) (Figure 2a) as a substrate for DAT, although its ability to be transported by SERT is not as efficient. Therefore, Solis et al. characterized a series of fluorescent analogues. Like ASP+, they were based on 1-methyl-4-phenylpyridinium (MPP+) with the aim of identifying a fluorescent SERT substrate. As a result of these efforts, APP+ 4-(4-(dimethylamino)phenyl)-1-methylpyridinium (Figure 4d) exhibited superior fluorescence uptake in hSERT-expressing HEK293 cells compared to other MPP+ analogs tested and was Na+- and Cl:dependent. Furthermore, addition of 5-HT induced an immediate decrease in APP+ accumulation, further demonstrating APP+ uptake was mediated by hSERT. Finally, APP+ signal was diminished in a concentration dependent manner by the SSRI fluoxetine.

The cocaine-based FLL JHC1-064 (Figure 1) as described before, is not selective among the MATs demonstrating identical binding affinities for rDAT (Ki = 16 nM) and rSERT (Ki = 16 nM). Hence, JHC1-64 could also be used to visualize SERT. Initial studies utilizing JHC1-064 in an heterologous system, revealed different levels of SERT oligomers in HEK293 cells which apparently can associate up to a pentameric form. In addition, as performed with DAT, JHC1-064 was also used to analyze internalization and the post endocytic fate of SERT showing a constitutive internalization mechanism and like DAT, after internalization SERT is primarily sorted to late endosomes and lysosomal compartments.

Even though, JHC1-064 binds with high affinity to SERT and was successfully used to study this transporter, in 2013, the Newman group explored the possibility of synthesizing a preferential SERT FLL by replacing the parent ligand MFZ2-12 on JHC1-064 with the SSRI, (+-)-citalopram (Figure 4e). Synthesis of ZP 455 (compound 8 in Zhang et al.) was achieved by modifying the 5-position of the dihydroisobenzofuran ring of (+-)citalopram, incorporating an aniline that served as a handle for the introduction of the Rhodamine Red-X fluorophore using an ethyl amino linker (Figure 4f). This FLL inhibited [3H]5-HT uptake in COS-7 cells transiently transfected with hSERT (Ki = 225 nM) and showed selectivity over hDAT (Ki =10,900 nM) and hNET (Ki = 11,800 nM). Confocal microscopy experiments were performed in a HEK293 stable cell line expressing EGFP-hSERT where visualization of hSERT by ZP 455 was demonstrated at a 20 nM.

Although, ZP 455 demonstrated remarkable selectivity for SERT, it was later revealed that staining SERT in neurons was not optimal and perhaps by increasing the binding affinity for the transporter, this could be improved. Hence, four novel FLL based on the eutomer (S)-citalopram were synthesized, exploring the addition of Rhodamine Red-X either in the tertiary amine of (S)-citalopram or as with ZP 455, in the 5-position of the dihydroisobenzofuran ring. As a result, three of the four newly synthesized compounds revealed higher inhibition of [3H]5-HT uptake in COS-7 cells transiently transfected with hSERT when compared to ZP 455. VK2-83 (compound 14 in Kumar et al. Figure 4g) showed the highest affinity(Ki = 34 nM) in the series. None of the compounds showed any uptake inhibition in hDAT or hNET transfected COS-7 cells. In addition, compared to JHC1-064 where incorporation of the Rhodamine Red-X dye resulted in a loss of binding affinity compared to the parent ligand, MFZ2-12, competition binding experiments utilizing [3H] (S)-citalopram remarkably revealed a Ki= 3.0 nM for VK2-83, which is nearly identical to the parent ligand, (S)-citalopram (Ki = 2.6 nM) under these conditions. It is important to mention two aspects that might have played a role for the increase in hSERT affinity when compared to ZP 455: 1) the utilization of the eutomer (S)-citalopram and 2) even though ZP 455 incorporated the fluorescent dye in the 5-position, there is an aniline moiety between the parent ligand and the linker of the fluorescent dye, whereas in VK2-83, the linker to the fluorescent dye was directly attached to the parent ligand structure (Figure 4f-g). Importantly, VK2-83 was able to label hSERT in HEK293 transiently transfected with EGFP-SERT (Figure 5).
Norepinephrine transporter (NET)

An early NET fluorescent ligand discovery effort proposed a series of ten fluorescent compounds based on the NE substrate analogue, m-iodobenzylguanidine (MIBG), and the inhibitors (-)-(2R,3S)-cocaine and nisoxetine with the purpose of generating fluorescent tools for neuroblastoma imaging. Neuroblastoma, the most common pediatric extracranial tumor has a sympathetic nervous system origin and 90% of neuroblastoma cells express NET. This study was supported by the successful use of radiolabeled [123I]MIBG or [131I]MIBG for diagnosis or treatment of neuroblastoma and pheochromocytoma. The generation of NET-directed fluorescent compounds was predicted to result in alternative diagnostic tools. The fluorescent labeling used for these ligands was mostly in the UV-Violet excitation window (350-420 nm). This excitation wavelength has several limitations including phototoxicity and thus utilization of these analogues could be limited.

Inhibition of [3H]NE uptake was performed utilizing human SK-N-SH-SY neuroblastoma cells. IC50 values for the synthesized compounds ranged from 0.03-1.32 muM. Compounds 8 and 9 (IC50 = 0.37-0.85 muM, respectively) and, in particular the MIBG analogue compound 4 (IC50 = 0.4 muM) (Figure 6a-c) with intermediate affinities were the most promising ligands in preliminary fluorescence experiments. The structures of the MIBG analogues and the (-)-(2R,3S)-cocaine analogues were very close to the parent ligands, and consequently this could explain the observation that these analogues retained comparable NET affinities. This contrasted with the nisoxetine-based ligands that were structurally dissimilar to the parent ligand, nisoxetine (Figure 6d) resulting in much lower affinities for NET.

Although, the MIBG fluorescent ligand possessed moderately high affinity for NET (IC50 = 0.4 muM), it was unclear whether the substrate profile was retained after tagging with the fluorescent label. Hence, Schwartz et. al utilized ASP+, which is described above as a substrate for DAT and SERT (Figure 2a). Initial fluorescent microscopy studies confirmed ASP+ as a substrate of NET in a Na+ dependent manner, and while this compound was capable of labelling surface expression of NET, it also accumulated in the cytoplasm of NET transfected HEK293 cells and in cultured neurons. Thus in addition to having utility for DAT and SERT, ASP+ became the first confirmed NET fluorescent substrate reported in the literature and was used as a tool to assess binding kinetics and transport stoichiometry by utilizing a combination of fluorescence methods such as fluorescent correlation spectroscopy (FCS), fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) and patch clamp.

Nevertheless, though ASP+ had a unique and preferential substrate profile for NET, it lacked selectivity with respect to DAT and SERT. Therefore, a series of stilbazolium analogues based on ASP+ were synthesized in one step yielding a preferential NET substrate, HNEP+ (Figure 6e). Interestingly, the hydroxy group played a fundamental role affecting both, transport and fluorescent properties of this compound, as NEP+ (Figure 6f) did not demonstrate intracellular accumulation in NET transfected HEK293 cells and had less bathochromic shift compared to its hydroxy analogue, HNEP+. Additionally, transport seemed to be highly affected by bulky compounds since dimers of ASP+ and HNEP+ were capable of labelling NET but no accumulation of these compounds in cells expressing the transporter was detected.

Another interesting characteristic of ASP+ is that it has an enhanced emission upon binding to NET, a feature that seems to not be present when binding DAT. This property appears to be influenced by the hydrophobic binding pocket of NET as these compounds seem to have a better quantum yield in apolar environments. Structurally, if ASP+ is compared to fluorescently labeled inhibitors such as JHC1-064, we can divide them into two pieces containing three features: 1) the cationic pyridinium moiety that might interact directly with the orthosteric binding site of the transporter serving as a parent ligand and, 2) the styryl moiety that serves as both, linker and electron rich substituents that plays a role in the fluorescent properties of these compounds.

JHC1-064 has been previously discussed as a FLL for labeling DAT and SERT in live cell systems. Indeed, as it binds to all three MATs, JHC1-064 has also been used to successfully label NET (rNET, Ki = 79 nM) in NET expressing HEK293 cells and in cultured noradrenergic neurons allowing cell surface expression to be visualized. As reported before for DAT and SERT, this FLL has a slow off-rate for all three MATs which is useful to study NET internalization mechanisms and post endocytic sorting in a heterologous cell system and in noradrenergic neurons. Successful labeling of NET in both systems and direct comparison of DAT and NET expressed in CAD cells, revealed differences in DAT and NET trafficking and post endocytic fate. Without a doubt, JHC1-064 has proven to be a powerful tool to study MATs.

Nevertheless, its usefulness for all three MATS has limitations when only one MAT is of interest. As with SERT, a new strategy based on the NET selective inhibitors, nisoxetine and talopram was recently reported. The lead FLL in this study, AC1-146 (compound 6 in , Figure 6g) is a nisoxetine-based fluorescent ligand tagged with Rhodamine Red-X, that unlike the nisoxetine analogues previously described for neuroblastoma imaging, the parent ligand structure is well conserved (Figure 6d). Thus, it is not surprising that its affinity for rat brain NET (rNET; Ki = 43 nM) is high. In addition, this fluorescent probe has an improved affinity for rNET when compared to JHC1-064 and is ~18-fold selective for rNET over rSERT (Ki = 785 nM) and ~36-fold selective over rat brain DAT (rDAT; Ki = 1540 nM). hNET, hDAT and hSERT binding affinities have not been reported. Nevertheless, initial confocal microscopy analysis revealed staining not only of hNET in a transporter expressing cell line, HEK293-YFP-NET (Figure 7) but in addition HEK293-YFP-SERT. In the same study, two attempts to generate a talopram-based fluorescent ligand were performed. The incorporation of the rhodamine tag yielded two fluorescent analogues that did not bind to rNET. Recently, AC1-146 was used to study oligomerization regulation of NET.
BEYOND DAT, SERT AND NET

Although, FLL used to study uptake-2 MATs is beyond the scope of this mini review, we want to highlight that it is well describe in the literature that ASP+ (Figure 2a) is a fluorescent substrate of OCTs. In fact, ASP+ was used to study OCTs before its application to study uptake-1 MATs. In addition, a structural analogue of ASP+, APP+ (also known as IDT307) (Figure 3d), has been used to study PMAT and this compound is also a substrate for OCTs, even thought ASP+ is not a substrate of PMAT. Although, ASP+ and APP+ have been useful fluorescent tools to study these systems, they have the caveat that both are substrates of uptake-1 MATs, therefore the development of selective ligands to study these transporters will increase our knowledge of the role of this supportive system in the regulation of monoamine signaling, also affording an oportunity to develop highly specific FLL substrates and inhibitors.
CONCLUDING REMARKS AND FUTURE CHALLENGES

The design and synthesis of novel fluorescent tools, in the form of small molecules with carefully appended fluorophores, has expanded in breadth and functionality, in part due to advances in microscopy and techniques such as dSTORM. In addition to novel fluorophores that allow a wide range of excitation wavelengths and the possibility of using more than one FLL in the same study provides exciting avenues for future research. Although ASP+, JHC1-064 and MFZ9-18 have proven to be important FLL for DAT, they also bind to SERT and NET, which limits their utility for visualizing DAT alone. Successful discovery of SERT and NET-selective FLL e.g., VK2-83 for SERT and AC1-146 for NET has provided important fluorescent tools for selective visualization of these MATs. Current efforts to identify highly DAT-selective FLL is underway and will be reported in due course. It is enticing to think that these compounds may have potential utility as diagnostic tools for diseases that directly or indirectly impact MATs. Thus, developing the MAT FLL beyond research tools and into potential diagnostics for the future is another exciting possibility of these molecules. The future for illuminating MATs with the next generation of novel FLL is bright.

passages.text: Determination and prediction of standardized ileal amino acid digestibility of wheat in broilers

This experiment evaluated the standard ileal digestibility (SID) of amino acids (AA) in 8 different sources of wheat fed to broilers and established prediction equations based on the chemical properties of wheat. A total of five hundred forty 1-day-old broilers were tested in 2 stages (from d 10 to 13 and from d 25 to 28). On d 13, 324 broilers were randomly assigned to 9 diets (6 replicate cages, 6 broilers per cage); on d 28, 216 broilers were randomly assigned to 9 diets (6 replicate cages, 4 broilers per cage). The 9 experimental diets included 8 test diets and 1 nitrogen-free diet. Titanium dioxide was added as an exogenous indicator at 0.5% of the diet. In 8 wheat samples, the mean values of total amino acids (TAA), dispensable amino acids (DAA), and indispensable amino acids (IAA) were 12.16% (CV 13.70%), 7.97% (CV 15.49%), and 4.20% (CV 11.47%). On d 13, the lowest SID of AA was Lys (86.71%), and the highest was Pro (97.98%). On d 28, the lowest SID of AA was His (81.31%), and the highest was Pro (96.83%). There was an effect of wheat source on the SID of AA except for Trp (P < 0.05); the broiler age had an effect on the SID of AA except for Tyr (P < 0.05); the SID of most AA were higher at d 13 compared to d 28. At d 13, the SID of AA was correlated with CP, NDF, and ST (P < 0.05). At d 28, the SID of AA was correlated with EE, Ash, ADF, and NDF (P < 0.05). The R2 value of stepwise regression equations to predict the SID of AA at d 13 was highest for Leu (R2 = 0.972), lowest for Asp (R2 = 0.785); at d 28 was highest for Gly (R2 = 0.995), lowest for His (R2 = 0.678). In conclusion, this experiment showed that the chemical properties of wheat can be used to establish accurate equations for predicting the SID of AA. This made it more efficient to obtain the SID of AA for wheat.
INTRODUCTION

Corn and soybean meal are commonly used in the preparation of feed, but their prices have risen in the past two years and are unstable. As a result, other suitable raw materials should be used in place of corn, soybean meal, and other raw materials in the feed formula to reduce costs and improve economic benefits.

Wheat is increasingly being used in livestock production. However, different breeds and growing environments may cause differences in their chemical properties, which affect the intake, digestion, and utilization of nutrients by poultry. To use wheat for precise diet configurations, it is vital to accurately determine the amino acid digestibility of wheat in poultry.

There are two commonly used methods for assessing the digestion and utilization of amino acids (AA) in poultry: apparent ileal digestible of amino acids (AIDAA) and standardized ileal digestible of amino acids (SIDAA). SIDAA accounts for the ileal endogenous amino acid (IEAA) flow, which is more appropriate for evaluating the utilization of AA in poultry. However, determining the SIDAA of the raw material is a very complicated procedure.

Many scholars have established equations that predict amino acid digestibility based on the chemical properties of raw materials, and the establishment of similar equations for wheat will make its use in poultry more efficient. Therefore, this study aims to determine the standardized ileal digestibility (SID) of AA of wheat in broilers at d 13 and 28, and to establish regression prediction equations based on chemical properties.

The study was approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of the China Agricultural University (permit number: AW11112202-1-2).

A total of seven hundred twenty 1-day-old male broilers (Arbor Acres) were obtained from commercial hatcheries and were fed standard commercial diets during the non-experimental period. Broilers were provided ad libitum access to water and feed throughout the experiment. The experimental diets included 8 test diets and 1 nitrogen-free diet (NFD) (Table 2). In the test diets, wheat was the only source of CP and AA. The NFD was used to measure the IEAA. The analyzed properties of the test diets are shown in Table 3. Titanium dioxide was used as an exogenous indicator in each experimental diet; vitamins and minerals were supplemented to meet or exceed the estimated nutrient requirements for broilers as recommended by the NRC. Each diet was fed for 3 D before ileal content collection on d 13 and 28. The broilers in 6 replicate cages (n = 6 broilers per cage) were euthanized, and the ileal contents were collected on day 13. The remaining broilers were fed the standard commercial diet until d 25 when 216 broilers were randomized to 6 replicate cages (n = 4 broilers per cage) for each experimental diet. Broilers were euthanized, and the ileal content were removed on d 28.

All euthanasia was performed by injecting pentobarbital, and all ileal digesta from the lower half of the ileum were collected by gently flushing with distilled water into aluminum containers. The ileum is defined as the part of the small intestine that extends from Meckel's diverticulum to the proximal ileocecal 40 mm. The ileal digesta from all broilers with a cage were pooled and frozen immediately after collection and subsequently freeze-dried. The dried ileal digesta were stored in a refrigerator at -4 C until required for chemical analysis.
Measurements

Dry matter (DM), crude protein (CP), crude ash (Ash), crude fiber (CF), and ether extract (EE) were analyzed according to analytical methods (934.01, 990.03, 920.39, 978.10, 942.05, respectively). Neutral detergent fiber (NDF) and acid detergent fiber (ADF) were determined using an Ankom220 Fiber Analyzer (Ankom Technology, NY) following a modification of the procedures described by.

The AA content of wheat samples, experimental diets, and ileal digesta were analyzed by the Ministry of Agriculture Feed Potency and Safety Supervision, Inspection and Testing Center (Beijing) (method 982.30). The titanium dioxide content in experimental diets and ileal digesta was measured as described by.

Statistical Analysis

All analyses were performed using SPSS25.0 software. The data were analyzed using one-way ANOVA. The cage and wheat sample were the experimental units for analyzing the data. Means were compared using the Tukey's studentized range test. The relationship between chemical properties and SIDAA values was analyzed using bivariate correlation analysis by SPSS procedure. The forward stepwise regression method was used to establish linear regression equations for predicting the SIDAA values from the chemical properties of wheat. Differences were considered statistically significant at P < 0.05.
RESULTS
Chemical Properties of Wheat

The analyzed properties of the wheat samples are shown in Table 1. The content of CP, EE, Ash, CF, NDF, ADF, and ST were from 9.81 to 16.92%, 1.34 to 2.43%, 1.54 to 2.26%, 1.83 to 3.33%, 10.82 to 14.34%, 3.11 to 4.70%, 65.70 to 76.50%, respectively. The CV of all other properties except ST was more than 10%. Among the 8 sources of wheat, total amino acid (TAA) ranged from 10.36 to 15.81%, and CV was 13.52%. The content of indispensable AA (IAA) was from 3.60 to 5.41%, and the CV was 11.34%. The concentration of dispensable AA (DAA) was from 6.76 to 10.48%, and the CV was 15.30%.

For the SID of IAA, the lowest was His (81.31%), the highest was Ile (93.45%), and the average was 89.42%. For the SID of DAA, the lowest was Ala (84.88%), the highest was Pro (96.83%), and the average was 91.73%. The average SID of TAA on d 28 was 90.45%.

DISCUSSION

In the present study, there were great differences in the chemical properties of 8 sources of wheat. This indicated that the wheat samples were representative. Different properties of wheat can be attributed to the growing environments, variety, and so on. Based on chemical analyses, the W-6 sample appeared to be of better quality than others, with high TAA content. Generally, the chemical properties of the samples were within the range previously reported for wheat.

At d 13, the SID of Met, Leu, Lys, and Trp measured in this experiment were close to those reported by in 14-day-old broilers; the SID of Glu, Thr, Leu, and Arg were close to those reported by in 14-day-old broilers. At d 28, the SID of Ala, Glu, Met, Leu, Phe, and Lys were close to the values measured by in 28-day-old broilers. The SID of Glu, Ala, Cys, Pro, Met, and Leu were close to those reported by in 21-day-old broilers, and the value of Trp was similar to that reported by in 21-day-old broilers. Except for the AA already mentioned, the SIDAA values measured in our experiment differed from those reported in each literature.

Several factors may contribute to these differences. First, the different growing environments and varieties of wheat may be the primary factor. On d 13 and 28, we also found that the SID of some amino acids varied among wheat samples from different sources. Due to the different growing environments and varieties of wheat, different sources of wheat have different chemical properties. It had been shown that SIDAA was influenced by the protein content in wheat. The sources of wheat may also impact the anti-nutritional factors that have many adverse effects on SIDAA. Anti-nutritional factors can increase intestinal viscosity and encapsulate nutrients, reducing the digestibility of raw materials in broilers and thus affecting SIDAA. Secondly, it could be related to the breed of experimental broilers, as different strains have different physiological structures and digest AA differently. Finally, the variations in IEAA loss resulting from different ratios of corn starch to glucose or sucrose in nitrogen-free diet formulations may lead to differences in SIDAA.

Based on the results of this study, it was concluded that 14-day-old broilers had a higher SIDAA than 28-day-old broilers, and the SIDAA decreased with advancing age. According to the literature, there are different results of the effect of broiler age on the ileal digestibility of AA in raw materials. The results are the ileal digestibility of raw amino acids increased with broiler age, decreased with broiler age, and remained unchanged with broiler age. These contradictory experimental results may be due to the content of anti-nutritional factors in the feed raw materials and the development of the intestinal tract in poultry. The wheat samples in our experiment contain low anti-nutritional factors with almost no negative impact on the intestine, while the intestine of poultry reaches its maximum digestive and absorptive capacity at about 2 wk and then tends to decrease. So, the SIDAA is higher in younger broilers than in older broilers. However, the intestinal tract of young broilers is not fully developed, such as the small intestinal villi are not fully developed and the intestinal flora is not fully established. Older broilers have more mature intestinal tracts and are more tolerant to anti-nutritional factors. The SIDAA for feed ingredients containing higher anti-nutritional factors was higher in older broilers than in younger ones.

The effect of the chemical properties of wheat on the SID of some AA was variable. For example, on d 28, the SID of Ile was positively correlated with CP, while the SID of Leu was negatively correlated with CP. The results are in agreement with the results reported by in corn distillers dried grains with solubles (DDGS) and in sorghum. These may be due to the different digestion processes of the various amino acids. In the process of establishing the prediction equation, we found that using only one predictor cannot establish the prediction equation for the SIDAA in wheat. In addition, with the introduction of predictors in the equation, the predictive ability of the equation has been improved. These suggested that the SIDAA in wheat may be influenced by multiple chemical properties.
CONCLUSIONS

The results of this study indicate that chemical properties and the SID of most AA in wheat showed a huge difference. Wheat source and broiler age can affect the SIDAA of wheat. There was a correlation between SIDAA and the chemical properties of wheat. We could develop the prediction equation for SIDAA based on the chemical properties of wheat samples.

passages.text: Sensory-processing sensitivity versus the sensory-processing theory: Convergence and divergence

Two individual-difference theories focus on sensory sensitivity: one emanating from psychology:sensory-processing-sensitivity (SPS); and one from occupational therapy:sensory processing theory (SP). Each theory is coupled with its measure: the highly-sensitive-person scale (HSPS) and the adolescent adult sensory profile (ASP). The constructs of both theories were claimed to be independent of neuroticism. To assess the convergence of these measures, we recruited participants from a general population and a Facebook Group dedicated to people high in SPS. The participants, N = 1,702 Mage = 26.9 (66.7% female), answered the HSPS, ASP, and neuroticism questionnaires. We subjected the HSPS and the APS to exploratory graph analysis. To assess the divergence of these measures from neuroticism, we performed meta-analyses. We also used a subsample obtained in an unrelated study, N = 490, to correlate HSPS and APS with the Big Five and additional measures. The results suggested that (a) the latent structure of these measures conforms to the theories only partially, (b) some of the sub-scales of these two measures correlated highly, r = 0.63, but low enough to suggest divergence, (c) both differentially predict membership in a Facebook group, and (d) both are not isomorphic with neuroticism. We concluded that HSPS primarily measures the emotional reaction to sensory stimulation, whereas ASP the behavioral reactions. We offer shorter yet reliable measures for both theories.
Introduction

All living organisms respond to variations in their physical environment through sensors that detect changes in energy patterns (such as light or sound). The likelihood of detection of changes in the environment depends on individual differences. Such individual differences are the subject of two theories:Sensory-Processing Sensitivity (SPS) and the Sensory processing theory (SP). However, researchers of these theories work in relatively independent research areas, each with its conceptualization of the dimensions of these individual differences and measurement instruments. SPS research suggests three interrelated sub-constructs, and the SP theoretically offers four individual difference profiles. Thus, our first goal is to test the presumed dimensions of SPS and SP, and our second goal is to test whether the measures emanating from these theories converge or diverge. Next, it is unclear whether each of the measures associated with these theories diverges from neuroticism and other related traits. Thus, our third goal is to establish divergent validity for the constructs of each theory. Finally, the SPS contains 27 items and the SP 60. Therefore, our last goal was to offer shorter versions for these scales to facilitate research covering the entire spectrum of phenomena described by the two theories. In summary, we investigated the measures of SPS and SP. Specifically, we (a) tested their dimensionality, (b) explored their similarities and uniqueness, (c) tested their divergent validity from neuroticism and other constructs, and (d) offered shorter and reliable versions of these scales.
Sensory-processing-sensitivity theory

The SPS theory, emanating from social and personality psychology, suggests individual differences in the capacity to process stimuli. People high in SPS (highly sensitive persons, or HSPs) notice subtleties and nuances in the environment that are not noticed by people low in SPS. On the other hand, HSPs can handle a smaller amount of stimulation than others. Therefore, HSPs are more likely to experience overarousal and to be overwhelmed. When HSPs are overwhelmed, they struggle to process the stimuli. Consequently, they experience intensive-physical reactions (such as rapid heart rate), which increases their overarousal. Their overarousal is increased until they attempt to block the stimulation:reach into transmarginal inhibition. The potential overarousal of HSPs may cause them to be more careful before responding to the environment.

The standard measures of SPS in human adults are the 27-item HSP scale (HSPS) and the short version of the 12-item HSPS questionnaire. Initially, the 27-items HSPS questionnaire was considered to reflect a single factor. However, further studies suggested three factors: (a) Ease of Excitation (EOE):becoming overwhelmed mentally by external and internal demands; (b) Aesthetic Sensitivity (AES):aesthetic awareness; and (c) Low Sensory Threshold (LST):unpleasant sensory arousal due to external stimuli. We sought to re-test the factor structure of the HSPS on a different, and larger, sample.
The sensory processing theory: Patterns of sensory processing

Another theory that pertains to a similar sensory pattern is Dunn's sensory processing theory, emanating from occupational therapy (SP). The SP theory, like the SPS theory, suggests individual differences in sensory processing but attributes these differences to high vs. low neurological thresholds and active vs. passive behavioral responses. Unlike the SPS theory, which focuses only on people high in sensory processing sensitivity, the SP theory considers the threshold of sensory processing and the behavioral response to sensations as separate continua: neurological thresholds for stimulation (high-low) and behavioral response (active-passive). These two axes underlie four sensory processing styles: (a) Sensory Sensitivity (Ss):a low neurological threshold that causes a strong physiological response but a passive-behavioral response with slow habituation to the sensation; (b) Sensory Avoiding (SA):a low neurological threshold that causes a strong physiological response, and an active-behavioral response to withdraw from the sensation (therefore quick habituation); (c) Low Registration (LR):a high neurological threshold that causes a weak physiological-response and a passive-behavioral response with delayed habituation to the sensation; and (d) Sensation Seeking (Se):a high neurological threshold that causes a weak physiological response, but an active-behavioral response that pursues sensation (therefore slow habituation).

The standard measure of SP in children is the 86-item Sensory Profile 2, and in adults is the 60-item Adolescent Adult Sensory Profile scale (ASP). A factor analysis of the ASP yielded 16 factors. used a scree test and suggested that the first four factors are similar to the theory. As predicted, it indicated factors of Low Registration and Sensation Seeking, but inconsistent with the theory, Sensory Sensitivity, and Sensory Avoiding items loaded together on two additional factors (, p. 78).
Sensory-processing sensitivity and sensory processing theory: Same or different?

The SPS and the SP theories lay on the same theoretical ground, suggesting that some people are more sensitive than others to sensory information. Therefore, some researchers refer to these two theories as the same or consider the SPS the same as the low neurological threshold profiles of the SP; Sensory Sensitivity or Sensory Avoiding.

Other researchers suggest that these theories should be distinguished. Their main argument is that while SP refers only to sensitivity to sensory stimulation, SPS refers to a deeper depth of processing, involving higher emotional arousal and empathic abilities. The high emotional arousal and empathic abilities cause aesthetic awareness of the environment's subtleties and nuances, such as delicate or fine scents, tastes, sounds, art, and music. Indeed, aesthetic awareness is one of the SPS factors labeled Aesthetic Sensitivity. Aesthetic sensitivity is not considered in the SP theory.

The debate regarding the convergence, or divergence, of the constructs of SPS and SP remained primarily theoretical. One exception is a study that reported that SPS was correlated with Low Registration, Sensory Sensitivity, and Sensory Avoiding, rs = 0.21, 0.50, 0.48, respectively, where Sensory Seeking was not correlated with SPS (; N = 116). These correlations are far from unity and may suggest divergence.

Moreover, both the SP and SPS theories suggest that although their respective constructs are related to neuroticism, they contain variances not shared with neuroticism. That is, the theories claim that their construct diverges from neuroticism. Therefore, we tested whether we could establish the divergent validity of SP and SPS with empirical data. We sought to determine whether neuroticism is only a sibling construct to SPS and SP or their identical twin. We probed this question (a) theoretically, (b) with meta-analyses, and (c) through data we collected.

Moreover, we expanded the probing of the divergent validity of SPS and SP to other candidate constructs whose measures may overlap with SPS and SP. First, we considered measures of all the Big Five traits rather than only neuroticism. Second, we considered specific constructs that may threaten the divergent validity of SPS and SP: trait anxiety, trait social anxiety, shyness, introversion (as part of the Big Five), attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), trait mindfulness, family environment, and attachment style. For example, we asked whether SP merely measures trait social anxiety. Suppose we establish that the correlations of neuroticism and all the other constructs with SPS and SP are low enough. In that case, we will establish the divergent validity of SPS and SP, providing evidence that they should be considered unique traits. Therefore, next, we review why neuroticism and the other constructs could overlap with SPS and SP.
Neuroticism

Neuroticism is defined as maladjustment or negative emotionality. Neuroticism is also called personality-negative affectivity or negative emotionality. Neuroticism is a temperamental sensitivity to negative stimuli and an inclination to experience psychological distress. It predisposes them to experience negative emotions, such as suffering more acutely from misfortunes. Moreover, neuroticism refers to a tendency towards experiencing tension, anxiety, depression, hostility, irrational thinking, impulsivity, self-pity, self-consciousness, low self-esteem, having unrealistic ideas, an inability to control urges, and inefficient ways of coping with stress.

passages.text: The authors of both SP and SPS theories discussed the relationship of the respective constructs with neuroticism. argued that neuroticism relates to the Sensory Avoiding profile, which refers to a low neurological threshold and an active behavioral response to stimuli. However, while Sensory Avoiding refers to a low neurological threshold for all stimuli, neuroticism definition refers only to sensitivity to negative stimuli. We did not find any study testing this argument.

argued that SPS is often, but mistakenly, considered as nothing more than neuroticism (e.g.,). On the one hand, SPS was correlated to neurotic personality traits, such as stress, anxiety, and depression. Also, neuroticism yielded positive correlations with SPS, and its component, especially with the SPS components of Low Sensory Threshold and Ease of Excitation . Nevertheless, Low Sensory Threshold and Ease of Excitation could be associated with negative emotions and experiences merely because their measures include many negatively worded items, describing negative consequences of greater depth of information processing.

On the other hand, SPS theory is compatible with other theories postulating individual differences in reacting both to negative and positive environments, such as differential susceptibility and biological sensitivity to context. Thus, SPS and other environmental sensitivity theories refer to a broader line of sensitivity to all kinds of stimuli, whereas theories about neuroticism refer specifically to sensitivity to negative stimuli. Therefore, the SPS-neuroticism correlation might be caused by the tendency of both HSPs and neurotic individuals to respond to stimuli cautiously. However, SPS is also theorized to reflect sensitivity to positive stimuli, unlike neuroticism, which refers only to sensitivity to negative stimuli. Consistent with the theories, brain research found that SPS is correlated with stronger reactions to positive images than to negative images, while neuroticism is associated with greater sustained medial prefrontal cortex for sad facial expressions, but not for happy or fearful facial expressions.

To address whether SPS is nothing more than neuroticism, we meta-analyzed all the relevant correlations with a random model. However, several correlations were reported by the same author. To account for the nesting of some correlations within an author, we used a three-level meta-analysis available in the metafor package in R. The mean-weighted correlation of SPS with neuroticism was  = 0.47, k = 21, N = 8,494 (see Supplementary Figure S1 in Section A). Our results are consistent with a meta-analysis conducted by,  = 0.40, k = 8, N = 6,790. In addition, a subsample of the studies in this meta-analysis, k = 11, N = 6,519, also reported correlations with SPS subscales and indicated that neuroticism correlates with Low Sensory Threshold,  = 0.30, Ease of Excitation,  =0.52, but barely with Aesthetic Sensitivity,  =0.12 (see Supplementary Figures S2, S3, and S4 in Section A). None of the analyses suggested that SPS and neuroticism are isomorphic. We sought to replicate these findings and test the correlations of SP components with neuroticism in data we collected to better understand the differences and similarities among SPS and ASP items.
Trait anxiety and trait social anxiety

HSPs were hypothesized to be at risk for adverse emotional and psychological outcomes. Indeed, SPS is correlated with anxiety, social anxiety, limitations in communication, and social phobia. Thus, we anticipate that trait anxiety and trait-social anxiety will also be positively correlated with subscales of SPS and SP related to sensitivity to negative stimuli (SPS: Ease of Excitation, Low Sensory Threshold, SP: Sensory Sensitivity, Sensory Avoiding, Low Registration). Nevertheless, given that sensory sensitivity applies to all kinds of stimuli, rather than mostly-anxious stimuli, we expect to find divergence between these concepts.
Shyness and introversion

The over-arousal characterizing HSPs' reaction to stimuli was theorized to lead to inhibition and social withdrawal. Social withdrawal and inhibition are social strategies mostly related to introversion and shyness. Therefore, argued that HSPs might be perceived as introverts or shy. Note that one of the HSPS scales contains an item about shyness: "When you were a child did parents or teachers seem to see you as sensitive or shy?." Not surprisingly, found positive correlations between shyness and SPS; r = 0.20, p < 0.001; r = 0.26, p < 0.001.

We meta-analyzed the relevant correlations we could find regarding introversion and SPS with a random model and found a positive correlation;  = 0.23, k = 21, N = 7,989 (see Supplementary Figure S5 in Section B). This result suggests that introversion is different from SPS. Therefore, we sought to replicate these findings and test the correlations of SPS and SP components with introversion and shyness.
ADHD

Both ADHD and SPS are often associated with unusual responses to sensory stimulations and include elements of emotional sensitivity, over-reactivity, and experiencing others' emotions as heightened. Moreover, SPS may also be related to inattention, a main symptom of ADHD, due to HSPs' tendency to experience over-arousal, pay attention to subtleties and nuances and be reactive to emotional stimuli.

On the other hand, ADHD also presents elements diverging from SPS, such as deficits in response inhibition, hyperactivity, and impulsivity, seeking self-stimulation, reduced empathy, and reduced ability to recognize emotions.

passages.text: found a positive correlation between ADHD and SPS; r (274) = 0.42, p < 0.001, and revealed, by exploratory factor analysis, two factors of ADHD, while one of them also contains all items of HSPS, suggesting that ADHD symptomatology may include elements of SPS, without this implying unity. We sought to replicate this finding and test the correlations of SPS and SP components with ADHD.
Trait mindfulness

Both SPS and mindfulness are related to sensitivity to environmental and internal sensations. However, the SPS's sensitivity to subtle stimuli is coupled with an unpleasant experience of overstimulation. In contrast, in mindfulness, the awareness of subtle stimuli is purposeful and nonjudgmental. Thus, it is not surprising that, unlike SPS, mindfulness correlates negatively with trait anxiety. Moreover, SPS was negatively correlated with mindful attention, awareness, and acceptance. Consequently, we predict that SPS would also correlate negatively with trait mindfulness. Yet, only the subscales pertaining to negative experiences should show this pattern.
Family environment and attachment style

argued that HSPs are prone to negative emotional outcomes, such as anxiety, only if they experienced a poor-family environment. They found that HSPs who recalled a troubled childhood were more introverted and emotional. Nevertheless, failed to find a significant interaction between negative childhood memories and SPS in predicting features of avoidant personality disorder. Moreover, found that SPS is an independent risk factor for experiencing psychological distress (depression and anxiety) above and beyond parental experiences. But still, an interaction was found between SPS and parental care when measuring depression. Although this last paper does not fully support, it still suggests that HSPs may be more sensitive to poor parenting than people low in SPS. Therefore, we explore whether the Perceived Social-Support of the entire family (PSS-Fa), specifically in childhood (up to the age of 18), is associated with SPS and whether it moderates the association of SPS with neuroticism.

An extension of the view that SPS is linked to childhood experiences can also be assessed with attachment styles. We meta-analyzed the correlations found in these papers with a random model. The mean-weighted correlation of Sensory Sensitivity with Attachment Anxiety was  = 0.28, k = 3, N = 443, and with Attachment Avoidance was  = 0.18, k = 2, N = 310. Sensory Avoidance was related to Attachment Anxiety;  = 0.29, k = 2, N = 310, and Attachment Avoidance;  = 0.21, k = 3, N = 443. Low Registration was related to Attachment Anxiety;  = 0.23, k = 3, N = 443. Moreover, Sensory Seeking is generally reported as related to Secure attachment. Indeed,; N = 194) reported significant negative correlations of Sensory Seeking with both Attachment anxiety (r = -0.13, p > 0.05) and Attachment Avoidance (r = -0.24, p < 0.001). Regarding SPS, it was reported to have a significant positive correlation with Attachment Anxiety (; N = 116, r = 0.23, p < 0.05), and with an attachment subscale of Feeling Upset and Misunderstood by Parents (; N = 156, r = 0.30 p < 0.01). Therefore, we sought to determine whether attachment styles are correlated with sensory sensitivity and moderate the association between SPS and neuroticism.
Overview

We set to address four questions: (a) What are the dimensions underlying the measures of SPS and SP? (b) To what degree do these measures and their dimensions converge? (c) Can divergent validity of SPS and SP be established when correlated with neuroticism and other candidate constructs? (d) Is it possible to offer a short and reliable version for measuring SPS and SP? To test our questions, we collected two samples. In the second sample, we measured the HSPS, ASP, Big 5, Shyness, ADHD, trait anxiety, trait social anxiety, trait mindfulness, family environment, and attachment style. We obtained ethical approval from our University's Ethics Committee for collecting both samples and obtained informed consent from all participants. In one sample, we measured the HSPS, ASP, three items of neuroticism, and membership in the HSPs Facebook group.

Next, we combined both samples and explored the dimensionality of their items with exploratory graph analysis (EGA). Based on the EGA, we removed items showing poor item stability and constructed new sub-scales reflecting various aspects of sensory sensitivity based on the stable items. Armed with these new scales, we tested the divergent validity of SPS and SP from neuroticism and other scales.
Materials and methods
Participants and procedure

We collected two samples of Israeli participants that were asked to participate in a study designed to learn about highly sensitive people. We provided all the participants with a link to a Qualtrics survey and asked them to fill out the HSPS, the ASP measure, the neuroticism measure, and a few demographic questions (see Figure 1). In the first sample, we recruited 1,340 students and volunteers. In the second sample, we recruited 490 first-year undergraduate students to participate in a laboratory experiment. Students participated in exchange for course credit. The experiment is not completed yet, and we extracted personality data collected before participating in the experiment. Of these, 128 (7%) had three or more missing items in any of the HSPS, ASP, or Neuroticism items. We deleted these participants' data and imputed missing data on HSPS and ASP, with mean substitution, for those with one (138) or two missing items (34).
Flowchart of number of participants.

The respondents in the combined sample, N = 1,702, include 1,147 first-year undergraduate students and 555 volunteers, Mage = 26.9 (66.7% female). The students participated in the study in exchange for course credit. The volunteers were recruited with snowball sampling via Facebook. A request to volunteer for this study was shared on several Facebook Groups (with the consent of the groups' managers). Importantly, one Facebook Group that yielded 187 responses was a group of Highly Sensitive People in Israel.1
Measures

We translated all the questionnaires to Hebrew and had a graduate student back-translated the items to English. Based on the back translation, the authors resolved minor discrepancies. To increase the validity of all scales, we presented all items on 11-point scales ranging from 0 = Not true at all to 10 = Very true, as more points on the scale enhance validity. Using 11-point scales has the drawback of not allowing comparison of the means in our study to the means of the measures reported by others. However, 11-point scales can increase the observed correlations among all items and reveal stronger correlations between SPS, SP, and all the constructs threatening their divergent validity. Thus, we used 11-point scales to provide the most rigorous divergent-validity tests.
Highly sensitive person
We used the 27-items HSP Scale (HSPS). The HSPS is reliable and widely used in HSPs studies.
Adolescent adult sensory profile
We used the 60-item ASP scale, based on Model of Sensory Processing. The ASP scale includes 15 items for each of the four sensory profiles and is widely used in adult sensory studies.
Neuroticism

In Sample 1, we used a 3-item neuroticism scale by, as was done in some SPS studies. The items were "Are you a tense or worried person by nature?," "Are you prone to fears?" and "Are you prone to depression?." In Sample 2, we used the Big Five (see below).
Trait anxiety
We used 20 items regarding trait anxiety from the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI), widely used for assessing trait anxiety.
Trait-social anxiety
We used the 20-item Social Interaction Anxiety Scale (SIAS). SIAS is a reliable measure of adults' trait-social anxiety.
Shyness
We used the 20-item Shyness Scale, a validated measure of shyness.
Big-five

We used the 44-item Big-Five Inventory (BFI). The BFI contains five scales for the five-trait model: Neuroticism, Extraversion, Openness, Agreeableness, and Conscientiousness. BFI scales include 8-10 items each and are reported to have high internal consistency reliabilities.
ADHD

We used the 20-item Barkely Deficit in Executive Function Scale-Short Form (BDEFS-SF) and the 6-item Adult ADHD Self-Report Screening Scale for DSM-5 (ASRS-5). Previous studies demonstrated excellent internal consistency for BDEFS-SF and excellent psychometric properties for DSM-5's Self-Report Screening Scale (sensitivity, 91.4%; specificity, 96.0%; AUC, 0.94). We used these instruments because ADHD is often under-identified in the adult population.
Trait mindfulness

We used the 15-item Mindful Attention Awareness Scale (MAAS) to assess dispositional mindfulness. MAAS has been validated for use with adults, and its internal consistency levels were found to be acceptable.
Family-support
We used the Perceived Social Support-Family Scale (PSS-Fa). Participants were asked to answer this measurement regarding their childhood (up to the age of 18).
Attachment styles
We used A Brief Version of the Experiences in Close Relationships Scale (ECR-12).
Analysis

Typically, researchers use exploratory factor analysis, or multi-dimensional scaling, to uncover the factorial structure of items of questionnaires. However, these techniques are less accurate and informative than the relatively new exploratory graph analysis (EGA).2 First, EGA is more likely to uncover the correct number of factors underlying the data. In EGA, the factors are called communities. Second, EGA estimates its solution's stability concerning the number of communities and the allocation of each item into a community. This feature allows the identification of unstable items that could be discarded from final analyses (conceptually similar to items loaded on multiple factors). Discarding unstable items makes the differences between the subscales stronger, but more accurate, and may provide shorter measurements. This is suitable for both ASP and HSPS because previous studies of these measurements reflect more than a single factor. Last, EGA provides a graphical output showing the degree of (dis)similarity between the communities and the items within them.

Technically, we bootstrapped our results over 500 samples using the bootEGA function in the EGAnet package in R (v.0.9.5). We used EGA to uncover the data structure via a network graph without assuming a simple structure (exploratory factor analysis seeks a solution with a simple structure). This approach is suited to test empirical dimensions in multi-dimensional data, and thus can test SP theory of two underlying dimensions, and may help solve the debate regarding the convergence, or divergence, of the constructs of SPS and SP. Based on EGA results, we constructed sub-scales of HSPS and ASP, computed their correlations with each other and the measured traits, and used them all to predict belonging to the HSP-Facebook group, using logistic regression.

The EGA bootstrapping provides information about the likely true number of communities (factors) underlying the data and the stability of the items (the percent of the time that a given item appears in the same community across the samples). The best estimate of the number of communities is the median across bootstrapped samples, as used here. As per item stability, it is recommended to retain items with stability between 0.65 and 0.75. Our first EGA yielded many items with lower stability. Therefore, we discarded unstable items with three iterations. First, we ran EGA on all items and discarded those with stability below 0.55; next, we re-ran EGA on the surviving items and discarded those with stability below 0.65; and, finally, we re-ran EGA once more without items with stability below 0.75.
Results

To facilitate the interpretation of our results and comparison to past findings, we labeled each of the 60 ASP items based on their original classification into four profiles (Ss, SA, LR, and Se), and the 27 HSPS items based on the prior factor analyses (EOE, AES, and LST). We subjected these items to EGA with 500 parametric bootstraps and plotted the median solution, containing only the stable items that belonged to only one community (see Table 1). In the first run, the bootstrapping indicated that four to eight communities might underlie the data with a median of six (40.2% of the samples). It also indicated that 22 of the 87 items had stability below 0.55. After dropping these items, the bootstrapping indicated that four to seven communities might underlie the data with a median of six (94% of the samples). Still, two items had stability below 0.65. We dropped these two items. Without these, the bootstrapping indicated the same number of communities with a median of six (92% of the samples). Still, three items had stability below 0.75. After dropping these three items, the conclusion did not change with a median of six communities (89% of the samples; median CI [5.32, 6.68]). All the remaining 60 items have good stability (see Figure 2). Figure 3 shows the network of the SPS and SP items and their underlying six communities: two containing HSPS items and four ASP items. Thus, the EGA differentiates clearly between HSPS and ASP.
EGA loadings table of the six HSPS and ASP sub-scales (without the unstable items).

Although eliminating unstable items would seem to make the differences between all subscales of HSPS and ASP stronger, EGA provided communities containing mixed subscales. Regarding the HSPS communities, the EGA suggested a clear separation of the Aesthetic Sensitivity items but an inconclusive division between Low Sensory Threshold and Ease of Excitation. Regarding the ASP, the EGA differentiated the Sensation Seeking and the Low Registration items but did not differentiate between Sensory Avoiding and Sensory Sensitivity. This finding is similar to the results reported by. There was no evidence for differentiation between the Sensory Avoiding and Sensory Sensitivity profiles. Instead, our results suggest that the items of the Sensory Sensitivity and Sensory Avoiding subscales are divided by auditory versus non-auditory sensitivity.
Short scales for HSPS and ASP

Based on the EGA, we constructed new short scales and subscales: A total HSPS 23-item scale, alpha = 0.92, AES with five items, alpha = 0.72, EOE and LST subscale with 18 items, alpha = 0.92, a total ASP 35-item scale, Se with 10 items, alpha = 0.68, LR with seven items, alpha = 0.72, non-auditory Ss-SA with 12 items, alpha = 0.75, auditory Ss-SA with six items, alpha = 0.84 (see Supplementary Appendix A).

We subjected the above new scales and subscales to item-response theory (IRT) analyses using the ltm package in R. IRT analyses might help to offer even shorter scales/subscales. We ordered the items based on the amount of information each item contained in the entire item range. Next, we constructed one-item subscales based on the item with the highest information and added items one at a time until we obtained Cronbach's alpha of 0.90 or ran out of items. We found that reducing the 18 EOE and LST items to nine still retains alpha of 0.90. No other subscale could be improved. Therefore, we used the short EOE and LST to construct a short total HSPS 14-item scale, alpha = 0.90. For items composing the short scales, see Supplementary Appendix A.3

When items are complex (or unstable), it could be either because they genuinely share cross-domain variance or have poor psychometric properties. One way to tease these possibilities is to inspect the scale's internal consistency. The full 27-item HSPS scale has identical Cronbach's alpha to the 23-item version based on the EGA (both are 0.92). Thus, the four items are redundant. Moreover, Cronbach's alpha of the 14-item scale we propose is 0.90, which is pretty good on its own, and demonstrates that the unstable items do not particularly contribute to the measurement of HSPS. Yet, the remainder of our analyses used the 18-item EOE and LST to benefit from its slightly improved reliability, alpha = 0.92 (see Supplementary Appendix B).

Interestingly, a short 12-item version was already suggested for the 27-items HSPS and was mentioned in passing by. Past applications of that short version yielded alpha's = 0.85. We compared this 12-item scale to the 14-item scale developed here. Nine items were identical, while our reliance on the item information replaced three items.4
Divergent validity for the HSPS and ASP

To test the divergent validity of the HSPS and ASP, we first considered Sample 1. We correlated the HSPS and ASP with neuroticism, age, gender, and membership in the HSP Facebook group (yes/ no). We also controlled (covaried out) neuroticism from age, gender, and HSP-Facebook-group membership. For predicting neuroticism and age, we used multiple regression, and for Facebook membership and gender, we used logistic regression.

As shown in Table 2, the disattenuated correlation of HSPS and ASP subscales and neuroticism are 0.80 or below. For EOE and LST subscale, the disattenuated correlation with neuroticism is 0.80, which indicates a marginal problem with divergent validity. To further probe the divergent validity of HSPS, we regressed the membership in the HSPS Facebook group on neuroticism and HSPS (using logistic regression). As shown in Model 1 in Table 3, the main effect of HSPS on Facebook membership is preserved when controlling for both neuroticism and ASP. Specifically, for every increase in one unit on HSPS, the likelihood of belonging to the HSP Facebook group increases by OR = 4.03, p < 0.001, controlling for the other predictors. Model 2 in Table 3 shows that both HSPS subscales predict membership in the HSP Facebook group controlling for neuroticism. Finally, when controlling for neuroticism, Model 3 in Table 3 shows that both the non-auditory and auditory ASP subscales are positively related to the likelihood of membership in the HSP Facebook group and that the LR scale is negatively related to it. Yet, the effects of the ASP subscales, controlling for neuroticism, are weak relative to the effects of the total HSPS scale, consistent with the low correlations of Se and LR with neuroticism (Table 2).
